passage.text: If you have ever stood outside on a stormy day, you know that the wind is a powerful force. Strong winds can blow down trees and even pick up heavy objects like cars. The power of the wind can also be harnessed to help people. In fact, humans have been capturing and using the wind's mighty power for thousands of years.

In ancient Egypt, the wind was an important source of power for transportation. Historians believe that the Egyptians were the first humans to create boats with wind-catching sails. They used these sailboats to travel quickly on the Nile River. Eventually, the Egyptians even used the wind to sail across the Indian Ocean.

Of course, transportation was not the only way that wind was used by people in the past. Humans discovered many other uses for wind, especially after the invention of the windmill. Windmills are machines with several fan-like blades. When the wind pushes against the blades, the blades spin and put other parts into motion. Thousands of years ago, the Persians first created windmills to help them water crops and grind grain. Later, the Dutch used windmills to pump water out of wetlands in order to have dry land for farming. Then, in 1888, an American named Charles F. Bush invented a way to use windmills to create electricity.

Humans are still using the wind to create electricity today. However, many modern windmills, called turbines, are giants compared to the windmills of the past. They can reach hundreds of feet into the sky, and each blade can be as long as a football field. These turbines are often built in groups on open prairies, along hillsides, or even in shallow ocean water. Some of these "wind farms" make enough electricity to power thousands of homes.

Machines that use the wind are not just getting bigger. Researchers are also developing turbines so small that ten can fit on a single grain of rice. In some cases, these diminutive turbines can only be seen with a microscope. Scientists believe that hundreds of these turbines could someday be packed into small electronic devices like cell phones. If the phones ran out of power, they could be charged by waving them in the air. With these and other inventions, people continue to improve wind-catching technology to power the planet in both big and little ways.

passage.text: Picture a world where sending a message takes days, or even weeks. Imagine needing a horse or a boat to carry your words to someone in a different city. This is what life was like until the 1830s. That was when Samuel Morse invented a system for sending messages using a telegraph machine and Morse code.

Unlike modern telephones, telegraphs could not send voices or pictures. Instead, the telegraph sent bursts of electricity through a wire. Telegraph users pushed a button to make electricity flow through the wire. If a person just tapped the button, the telegraph sent a short burst called a "dot." If a person held down the button longer, the telegraph sent a longer burst called a "dash."

Samuel Morse invented a code to give meaning to these bursts of electricity. He gave each letter of the alphabet a different mix of dots and dashes. For example, if you wanted to send the letter A, you would send a dot followed by a dash. This system of dots and dashes came to be known as Morse code. passage.text: Have you ever wondered why a computer keyboard looks the way it does? Shouldn't the letters be in alphabetical order? Instead, the keys on most keyboards appear to be all mixed up. Most keyboards designed in this way are known as QWERTY keyboards. The name QWERTY comes from the first six keys in the top row of letters, moving from left to right. This style of keyboard is not just found on computers. Many keypads on tablets and cell phones also use the QWERTY design. Although it is found on modern devices, the QWERTY keyboard arrangement was actually invented back in the 1800s.

In 1868, Christopher Sholes invented the first modern typewriter. Typewriters were machines with letter keys on the ends of curved moving bars. When the typist hit a key, the bar would swing up and print a letter on a piece of paper. The keys on Sholes's first typewriter were arranged in alphabetical order. However, he soon changed the order of the letters to the QWERTY arrangement.

Some people think that Sholes chose the QWERTY design in order to prevent his typewriter from jamming. Keys next to one another would often stick when hit one after the other. So Sholes may have moved the keys to spread out the most-used letters. Others say that Sholes chose this design in order to help people type more quickly.

In 1893, the five main typewriter manufacturers decided to merge into one big business, the Union Typewriter Company. They all agreed to use the QWERTY keyboard on their typewriters. Over the years, people have tried to introduce different keyboard arrangements. The most famous was the Dvorak keyboard invented by August Dvorak in the 1930s. Many people agreed that it was a better keyboard arrangement because the most-used letters were all on the center row. But it was too late! The QWERTY keyboard had already been on most typewriters for over forty years.

Once personal computers became popular in the late twentieth century, the QWERTY keyboard layout could have been changed. After all, computer keyboards do not have curved moving bars that could cause keys to jam. However, even though we did not need to stick with the QWERTY keyboard, the QWERTY keyboard stuck with us. It has been around so long that it is hard for most people to imagine another way to type.

passage.text: Today, almost all American homes have a refrigerator. These devices are so common that it can be difficult to imagine life without one. However, most American kitchens actually did not have a refrigerator until the 1930s. When refrigerators finally arrived, they brought big changes to the way Americans stored and prepared their food.

In the past, people often worried about food safety. Foods like meats and vegetables can quickly go bad. Eating these foods after they have spoiled is not only unpleasant but also dangerous. Before people had refrigerators, they spent a lot of time pickling and drying fresh foods. Pickled and dried foods can last for months, and they do not need to be kept cool. Before refrigerators, foods like pickles and dried jerky were not just tasty treats. They were a way for people to stay fed in the winter when fresh food was not available.

People in the past also had to be more thoughtful about where they kept food that could not be preserved. They often stored foods in cool places like streams or underground cellars. People also used small boxes filled with ice for storing food. They bought the ice or cut it from frozen ponds or lakes. However, ice melted and had to be replaced, and it was difficult to find during warm months. So the invention of the electric refrigerator was a welcome change.

In the early twentieth century, it was unusual to find refrigerators in most American homes. However, the devices started to become more prevalent after World War II. By the 1960s, they had spread to nearly every home in America. Having a safe and dependable place to store food changed American lives. People no longer needed to pickle or dry food to prepare for winter. They did not have to buy ice or drag it from a lake. Instead, storing and preserving food became as simple as a quick trip to the fridge.

passage.text: In the 1940s, the people of Paramount, California stayed cool by visiting the Paramount Iceland Skating Rink. Frank Zamboni first opened the rink in 1940. Before long, it was filled with hundreds of happy skaters. Although business was good, Zamboni had a problem: the blades of people's skates would always make the ice become rough and uneven. Every few hours, the entire rink needed to be cleaned and smoothed. This job required four or five workers and about ninety minutes of work. Zamboni wanted a faster way to place a flat new sheet of ice on the rink.

It took Zamboni nine years to create a machine for this task. He named his creation the Zamboni Model A Ice Resurfacer. However, the machine eventually became known simply as the Zamboni. The first Zamboni was a strange-looking vehicle. It was built with parts from a truck, an oil well, and an airplane. Odd as it may have looked, it got the job done! Using this machine, one driver was able to create a fresh new layer of ice in about ten minutes.

It takes several steps to make an ice rink smooth, and a Zamboni can do them all. First, the Zamboni uses a sharp blade to scrape away the top layer of ice on the rink. Next, the Zamboni washes the skating surface and removes the dirty water. Then, it sprays out clean water from the back of the machine. Finally, it smooths the surface as the water freezes into a sheet of fresh ice.

In 1950, a famous ice skater named Sonja Henie saw the Zamboni in action. She liked it so much that she bought two of the machines. Soon, hockey teams started buying them as well. Then, in 1960, the Zamboni made its first appearance at the Olympic Games. That year, the U.S. hockey team won the gold medal playing on ice smoothed and cleaned by Zambonis. Today, fans of ice sports still love watching these machines change roughed-up skating surfaces into sleek sheets of flat, polished ice.
